analysis.one_liner: Bans political action committees from spending money in federal elections.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban political action committees from federal elections drew no cosponsors, was sent to committee the day it was introduced, and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Bob Inglis, a first-term Republican from South Carolina, proposed amending the Federal Election Campaign Act to stop political action committees — the pooled-money committees run by corporations, unions, and interest groups — from contributing to or spending money in federal elections [S2][S3]. The House referred it to the Committee on House Administration on the day it was introduced [S5]. No hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors followed, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 1995 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates for federal office who do not rely on PAC money — challengers, and any candidate who wants to run on small individual donations — would benefit from a level playing field. Voters would get a campaign finance system where House and Senate members raise money directly from individuals rather than through industry and union PAC committees.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 to prohibit contributions or expenditures by political action committees in federal elections [S2][S3].

It provides that no person other than a political committee or an individual may solicit, make, or receive contributions, or make expenditures to influence a federal election — cutting corporate, trade association, and labor PACs out of the channel entirely [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on PACs themselves — the corporate, trade association, labor, and ideological committees that bundle money for federal campaigns — and on incumbent members of Congress, who are the largest recipients of PAC contributions. Money would likely have shifted to individual donations, party committees, and independent spending.

drawbacks.text: Banning PACs does not cap total campaign spending: money can move to unlimited individual contributions within limits, party committees, and independent expenditures, so the bill might change the label on the money more than the amount [S3].

PACs also pool small individual donations — including union members' dues-based contributions — into a collective voice; a flat ban removes that channel for citizen groups as well as corporations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core goal — ending a system in which organized money from a few thousand PACs finances congressional campaigns — is real, and the bill takes a clean swing at it. But the one-page bill attacks only the PAC channel; it does nothing about party money, individual contribution limits, or independent spending, so its practical effect would likely be a reshuffling of the same money. The lack of even a single cosponsor suggests members of both parties saw little political value in cutting off a funding source they rely on.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Representative Inglis introduced the bill on August 2, 1993, and the House referred it to the Committee on House Administration the same day [S1][S5].
No further action was ever recorded on the bill, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs and the industries and unions that fund them keep their channel into federal campaigns, and incumbent members of Congress keep the PAC money they raise from them. Voters are left with the existing system.

for.name: Rep. Bob Inglis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate PAC activities in federal elections; it was his only action on the bill besides the referral.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over federal election law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 2, 1993 and took no further action — no hearing or markup was ever recorded on the bill.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership of the 103rd Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; a bill with no committee action and no cosponsors was never scheduled.

against.name: PACs and their sponsoring organizations
against.role: Corporate, trade association, labor, and ideological political action committees
against.what_they_did: Would have lost their legal channel for contributing to and spending in federal elections; the bill never advanced far enough to force a public fight over it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows the split; it drew no cosponsors from either party, offering no evidence of support on either side [S4].

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, trade association, labor, and ideological)
industries.note: The bill would have shut PACs out of federal elections entirely, ending a pooled-money channel that gives organized interests direct influence over campaigns. Because the bill died, PACs kept their role untouched.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress (as recipients of PAC money)
industries.note: Incumbents raise more PAC money than any other group and were the direct beneficiaries of the bill dying. The absence of even one cosponsor reflects how few members wanted to cut off their own funding pipeline.
